summary: Specifies how to use the AES-CCM and AES-GCM authenticated encryption algorithms with the CMS authenticated-enveloped-data content type. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This says how to use two kinds of strong lock-and-seal methods inside secure messages, so every program sets them up the same way.

questions: how to use aes-gcm in cms
what is cms authenticated enveloped data
subtitle: How to plug the AES-CCM and AES-GCM authenticated encryption modes into CMS authenticated-enveloped data.

tldr.problem: The CMS authenticated-enveloped-data content type needs a content-authenticated-encryption algorithm, and AES-CCM and AES-GCM need agreed identifiers, parameters and usage rules to be used consistently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns an object identifier for each AES key size and mode, defines the CCMParameters and GCMParameters structures (a nonce and a tag length), and requires automated key management so a nonce and key are never reused.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can encrypt and authenticate CMS content in one pass in an interoperable way, as long as each content gets a fresh key and a unique nonce.

today: RFC 5084 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be used with the authenticated-enveloped-data content type of RFC 5083.

sections.title: Two Authenticated Encryption Modes for CMS
sections.content:
This RFC sets the conventions for using AES-CCM (Counter with CBC-MAC) and AES-GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) as the content-authenticated-encryption algorithm in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) authenticated-enveloped-data content type, which is defined in RFC 5083.

CMS values are generated using ASN.1. AES comes in three key sizes: 128, 192 and 256 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Both methods put your message in a locked box and add a tamper seal. If anyone changes the box, the seal breaks.

sections.title: How CCM and GCM Work at the Interface
sections.content:
Both modes are generic authenticated encryption block cipher modes defined for any 128-bit block cipher; here they are used with AES. Each takes four inputs: an AES key, a nonce (called an initialization vector in GCM, but referred to as a nonce throughout), a plaintext and optional additional authenticated data (AAD). Each produces a ciphertext and an authentication tag, also called a message authentication code.

The nonce is generated by the party doing the encryption and MUST be unique within the scope of any key. The AAD is authenticated but not encrypted, so it is not part of the output. In CMS authenticated-enveloped data, the authenticated attributes make up the AAD.
sections.plainLanguage: Both methods put your message in a locked box and add a tamper seal. If anyone changes the box or the label on it, the seal breaks.

sections.title: Automated Key Management Is Required
sections.content:
Reusing a nonce with the same key destroys the security guarantees, so statically configured keys are hard to use safely. Implementations MUST use an automated key management system.

The four general CMS key management techniques all qualify, as long as a fresh content-authenticated-encryption key is generated for each content: key transport, key agreement, previously distributed symmetric key-encryption keys, and passwords. For other CMS techniques the properties are unknown, so designers must do their own analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: Never use the same one-time number with the same key twice. The easiest way to be safe is to make a brand-new key for every message.

sections.title: AES-CCM Parameters
sections.content:
AES-CCM has three object identifiers, one per key size: id-aes128-CCM, id-aes192-CCM and id-aes256-CCM. The identifier lives in the contentEncryptionAlgorithm field, and the parameters field MUST be present. The authentication tag goes in the mac field and protects both the authenticated attributes and the encrypted content.

CCMParameters holds an aes-nonce of 7 to 13 octets and an aes-ICVlen of 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 or 16 octets. The nonce holds 15-L octets, and L=8 is RECOMMENDED because a key normally protects a single content. The ICV length MUST match the size of the mac value, and 12 octets is RECOMMENDED. Neither content nor AAD needs padding.
sections.plainLanguage: The message carries a small settings card: which lock was used, the one-time number, and how long the seal is. The receiver reads it to open the box.

sections.title: AES-GCM Parameters
sections.content:
AES-GCM likewise has three identifiers: id-aes128-GCM, id-aes192-GCM and id-aes256-GCM, and the parameters field MUST be present. GCMParameters holds an aes-nonce and an aes-ICVlen of 12 to 16 octets.

The GCM algorithm permits a nonce of any number of bits from 1 to 2^64, but because it is an OCTET STRING it must be a multiple of 8 bits. Nonces within a key MUST be unique but need not have equal lengths. A 12-octet nonce is processed more efficiently, so that length is RECOMMENDED. As with CCM, the ICV length MUST match the mac value and 12 octets is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The second lock works the same way: the message carries a settings card with the one-time number and the seal length.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Counter mode gives strong confidentiality when used properly, and one cited analysis shows it is at least as strong as CBC mode with the same block cipher. It is easy to misuse, though. If counter block values are ever used for more than one encryption with the same key, the same key stream encrypts both plaintexts and confidentiality is voided. CMS authenticated-enveloped data supplies the tools to avoid this.

Generic precomputation attacks limit the theoretical strength of any block cipher in counter mode to 2^(n/2) bits for an n-bit key. Long keys are the best countermeasure, and an unpredictable nonce makes the attacker's table bigger.

Content-authenticated-encryption keys must be generated randomly. Weak pseudo-random number generators can leave little or no security, and RFC 4086 gives guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: If you reuse the same one-time number, a clever person could compare two locked boxes and learn what is inside. Fresh keys and good random numbers prevent that.
